Q: How to sort a list of object by two fields when the first field is a date but of string type and the second field is a plain string A:

For your specific case, your code works as-is and no change is necessary.

The String ordering of your date ("yyyy-MM-dd") matches the chronological ordering of those dates. That is one nice quality of that specific date format.

This is assuming all dates are between years 1 and 9999, which is highly likely to be the case.

Q: why data frame length greater than 16383 byte in http 2.0 A:

This is just a default of the HTTP2 spec (and SPDY spec that preceeded it.) There's not some technical limitation limiting it to 16KB; they set it low probably to save RAM on low-spec hardware (like microcontrollers where they decided to stick a web server in the device) and busy web sites. I think they also benchmarked things and found this size was large enough. HTTP2 does allow this value to be negotiated up as high as 16MB though.

Q: JwkSet gives Cannot resolve constructor 'JWKSet(List<RSAKey>)' - Stream.collect(Collectors.toList()) vs Stream.toList() A:

The JWKSet constructor accepts a List<JWK> as its constructor parameter. However, the value returned by your .toList() implementation is a List<RSAKey>, not a List<JWK>. Since Java generics are not covariant, a List<RSAKey> cannot be used here, even though RSAKey extends JWK.

Note that this would work if the creators of the library had made the constructor signature JWKSet(List<? extends JWK> keys) instead of JWKSet(List<JWK> keys), since a List<RSAKey> would be a valid argument for that signature.

The fix for this is to ensure the list you're passing in is the right type. This can be achieved by ensuring the stream you're calling .toList on is a Stream<JWK> and not a Stream<RSAKey>.

A simple approach is to use explicit type arguments when calling the Stream.map method to instruct the compiler to use JWK as the generic type for the method call, rather than the RSAKey type it's currently inferring based on the return type of RSAKey::toPublicJWK. This will result in a Stream<JWK> instead of your current Stream<RSAKey>.

JWKSet mySet2 = new JWKSet(keys
        .stream()
        .<JWK>map(RSAKey::toPublicJWK)
        .toList() );

Q: OCI SNS and SQS equivalent A:

Not really.

OCI Notifications + OCI Queue isn't a direct equivalent of SNS + SQS. OCI Queue is more like SQS (point-to-point messaging), while Notifications is mainly meant to deliver events to supported endpoints (Functions, HTTPS, email, etc.), not to fan out messages to multiple queues like SNS does.

So if you want one message to end up in multiple queues, the usual pattern is:

Producer
   ↓
OCI Notifications
   ↓
OCI Function
  ├─→ Queue A
  ├─→ Queue B
  └─→ Queue C

If your use case is more about multiple consumers reading the same stream of events, then OCI Streaming is probably the better fit. Yes, you'll still deal with concepts like partitions and consumer groups, but OCI manages the infrastructure, so you don't have to run Kafka yourself.

Q: Printing 9 lines counting from 0-9 not working A:

You are going to want to use for loops. Depending on if you want an int or string to print out there are two ways I can think of doing this while being as literal as possible about the answer.

If all you need is to print the numbers to the screen a string should suffice.

def countdown():
for i in range(0,9):        #Iterate for 9 lines
    x=""                    #Using string x
    for j in range(0,10):   #Iterate through numbers 0-9 which is actually ten digits
        x += str(j)         #convert the int j to a string and add it to string x
    print(x)

If your trying to output an int convert the string to int an before printing.

def countdown():
for i in range(0,9):        #Iterate for 9 lines
    x=""                    #Using string x
    for j in range(0,10):   #Iterate through numbers 0-9 which is actually ten digits
        x += str(j)         #convert the int j to a string and add it to string x        
    y = int(x)              #convert the string x to int y
    print(y)

In either case your shell should print this:

>>> countdown()
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789
0123456789

You were attempting to use a list which could achieve a similar result but not what you asked for.
